answer: I'd like to talk about a toy that kept me busy for most of my early childhood. A toy I absolutely adored as a child was a set of building blocks my parents gave me one birthday. They were bright plastic pieces in red, yellow and blue, packed into a bucket that seemed enormous to me at the time. My father brought them back from a trip to Dhaka, which made them feel even more special, since toys like that were hard to find in our town back then. It might sound simple, but it kept me endlessly [[entertained]] for years. I would spend hours constructing houses, towers and imaginary cities, completely lost in my own little world. Sometimes I tried to copy the bridge over the Jamuna, and it collapsed more times than I can count. What I loved was how the blocks allowed for endless creativity; I could build almost anything I could imagine. When my younger sister was old enough, I let her join in, and we built whole villages together on the living room floor. Looking back, I think that toy quietly [[nurtured]] my imagination and problem-solving skills. It was wonderfully [[engaging]] in a way that required real involvement, unlike the passive screens children have today. I have very fond, [[nostalgic]] memories of sitting on the floor surrounded by my creations. Honestly, I think the best toys are the ones that let children invent and build rather than just watch. That simple set taught me patience and creativity without my ever realising it. It remains one of the toys I remember most warmly from my childhood, and I would happily give one to a child today.

followUps.q: Do children today still play with toys like that?
followUps.answer: Some do, but many prefer tablets and phones. My four-year-old nephew in Dhaka absolutely loves building blocks, though, so perhaps they haven't completely lost their [[appeal]] after all.

followUps.q: Did you have any other favourite toys?
followUps.answer: I also loved a small plastic cricket bat that I used in endless matches with the neighbourhood children, usually until someone hit the ball over a wall and we had to go and apologise.
